titulo: Condicional compuesto: Forming the condicional compuesto

aula.objetivo: Form the condicional compuesto («habría ido») and use it to talk about what would have happened but didn't, to give advice and criticism about the past («yo en tu lugar habría…», «deberías haberlo dicho») and to express wishes that didn't come true («me habría gustado»).

itens.pt: could have, would have been able to
in your place, if I were you

blocos.titulo: Habría + participle: what would have happened
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: think of something you did NOT do in the past, but would have done in other circumstances. In English: "I would have gone", "I would have bought". STEP 2: this is another tense that maps neatly onto English: "would have" + participle = the conditional of «haber» + participle: «habría ido», «habría comprado». STEP 3: the conditional of «haber»: habría, habrías, habría, habríamos, habríais, habrían. The stem «habr-» is the same as in the future («habré»), and the «-ía» endings are those of the imperfecto of «comer» and «vivir» («comía, vivía»). Every form has an accent on the «í». STEP 4: the participle is the usual one: hablado, comido, vivido; hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, abierto, vuelto, roto. With «haber» it never agrees. STEP 5: the key use: an action that didn't happen, usually followed by the reason with «pero»: «Habría ido a la fiesta, pero tenía que trabajar» (I would have gone to the party, but I had to work). STEP 6: the same for what you "would have liked": «Me habría gustado viajar más» (I would have liked to travel more). Note: English often says "would have liked TO HAVE travelled"; Spanish keeps the simple infinitive: «me habría gustado viajar». STEP 7: negation and pronouns go before the auxiliary: «No lo habría hecho» (I wouldn't have done it), «Lo habría comprado». STEP 8: one letter changes everything: «había ido» (had gone: you did go, before something else) and «habría ido» (would have gone: you didn't). Listen carefully for «bía» versus «bría».
blocos.comparacao: "Would have + past participle" = «habría + participio»: «habría ido», «habría hecho». English "would" is never a separate word here — it's the «-ía» ending on «haber». The auxiliary is «haber», not «tener», and «había» (had) is one letter away from «habría» (would have).

tabela.exemplo: I would have gone with you.
You would have seen it from there.
They would have done it better.

erros.motivo: Every form of the conditional of «haber» has an accent on the «í».
The auxiliary is «haber»; English "would have" never becomes «tendría».

erros.errado: Ayer había ido al cine, pero tenía que trabajar.
erros.certo: Ayer habría ido al cine, pero tenía que trabajar.
erros.motivo: If you didn't go, it's «habría ido» (would have gone). «Había ido» (had gone) means you went.

blocos.enunciado: Say five things you would have done last weekend but didn't, and why: «Habría ido a la playa, pero llovía. Habría llamado a mi abuela, pero…»
Say out loud the simple conditional of the verbs you already know («iría, comería, viviría, podría, querría») and the participles of five verbs, including two irregular ones.
